introduction-the-kernel-bottleneck-revis.core: The Linux network stack is general-purpose: for every packet it allocates an sk_buff, runs netfilter hooks, routing, and protocol handling. That's great for flexibility but costs hundreds of nanoseconds. For simple decisions (drop this DDoS packet, forward that one) most of that work is wasted. The question is how to run custom fast-path logic early, without abandoning the kernel as DPDK does.

first_principles.problem: An iptables-based DDoS filter collapses at 5 Mpps because every packet goes through full stack processing before being dropped.
truths: Bypassing the kernel loses its benefits.

analogy.title: A bouncer at the car park entrance vs inside the club
analogy.story: Turning away troublemakers at the car park saves the effort of checking coats and IDs first.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers judge; eBPF programs follow verified code paths.

check.q: Why is dropping a packet in iptables more expensive than in XDP?
check.a: By iptables the kernel has already allocated an sk_buff and run part of the stack; XDP runs in the driver before that.

the-old-king-dpdk-kernel-bypass.core: DPDK (kernel bypass) achieves maximal throughput by taking the NIC away from the kernel and polling it from user space. It dominated telco and NFV, but it needs dedicated cores at 100%, a reimplementation of everything the kernel provides (ARP, routing, TCP and tooling), special drivers, and it can't easily share the NIC with normal applications. Those costs are why XDP gained ground.

first_principles.problem: A team adopts DPDK for a load balancer and then has to rebuild health checks, ARP, metrics and debugging tools from scratch.

analogy.title: Building a private railway
analogy.story: Fastest possible trains, but you must also build your own stations, signals and maintenance crews.
analogy.breaks: Railways serve many customers; a DPDK NIC serves only its app.

check.q: What's a major operational downside of DPDK?
check.a: You lose the kernel networking stack and standard tools, so you must reimplement or work without them.

the-new-challenger-xdp-express-data-path.core: XDP runs an eBPF program in the NIC driver at the earliest point a packet arrives, on the raw DMA buffer before sk_buff allocation. The program can drop it, pass it to the normal stack, bounce it back out the same NIC, redirect it to another NIC, CPU or AF_XDP socket, or modify it. Normal traffic still uses the kernel, so you get fast-path speed and kernel features together.

first_principles.problem: A DNS service wants to drop amplification attack packets at line rate while serving legitimate queries normally.
truths: The earliest hook is in the driver.
Raw buffers are cheap to inspect.
Passing to the stack keeps features.
derivation: Fall back to **generic mode** for testing.

analogy.title: A sorting machine at the loading dock
analogy.story: It kicks out junk immediately and sends good parcels into the building as normal.
analogy.breaks: Sorting machines are fixed; XDP programs are loadable at runtime.

how-xdp-works-actions-and-verdicts.core: An XDP program receives an xdp_md context with pointers to the packet's start and end, and must bounds-check every access. It can read and write the packet, adjust its head or tail (to add or remove headers for encapsulation), look up eBPF maps (blocklists, backends, counters) and call helpers. It returns DROP, PASS, TX, REDIRECT (via devmap, cpumap or xskmap to AF_XDP sockets) or ABORTED (an error, traced).

first_principles.problem: An engineer's XDP load balancer must encapsulate packets and forward them out another NIC to backends.
truths: Maps share state with user space.

analogy.title: A customs officer with a rulebook and a stamp
analogy.story: They inspect each parcel's label (headers), consult the rulebook (maps), re-label if needed and choose the exit.
analogy.breaks: Officers can improvise; programs only do what the verifier allowed.

check.q: How does user space change an XDP program's behaviour without reloading it?
check.a: By updating eBPF maps (e.g. blocklists, backend tables) that the program reads.

the-ebpf-verifier-safety-without-sacrifi.core: Before any eBPF program runs, the kernel verifier simulates every path. It rejects unbounded loops (only bounded loops are allowed), out-of-bounds memory access, uninitialised reads, invalid helper calls and excessive complexity. Then the JIT compiles it to native code. That's what makes it safe to run custom code in the kernel without crashing it, but it also explains cryptic 'invalid access' errors when bounds checks are missing.

first_principles.problem: An XDP program fails to load with 'invalid access to packet, off=14 size=20'.

analogy.title: A building inspector approving plans before construction
analogy.story: No construction starts until every structural path is proven safe.
analogy.breaks: Inspectors can approve exceptions; the verifier never does.

check.q: Why does the eBPF verifier reject a packet read without a data_end check?
check.a: It can't prove the read stays within the packet buffer, which could crash or leak kernel memory.

why-ebpfxdp-is-replacing-dpdk.core: XDP gets close to DPDK speeds for common tasks (drop, forward, load balance) while keeping the kernel: no dedicated polling cores (it's interrupt and NAPI driven), the NIC is shared with normal applications, standard tools work, programs reload live, and it runs on stock kernels. Facebook's Katran, Cloudflare's DDoS mitigation and Cilium all use it. DPDK remains for full user-space stacks and extreme per-core packet rates.

first_principles.problem: A team weighs DPDK versus XDP for a new L4 load balancer and DDoS layer.

analogy.title: A fast lane added to the existing motorway vs a private railway
analogy.story: The fast lane uses existing infrastructure and is nearly as quick for most journeys.
analogy.breaks: Fast lanes have fixed speed; XDP throughput depends on driver support.
